explanation: Perseus cut off her head while watching her reflection in a polished shield, so he never met her gaze. The winged horse Pegasus sprang from her body.

claims.text: In Greek myth, anyone who looked at Medusa was turned to stone.
Medusa's gaze turned people to stone, not to salt, ice or wood.
Perseus beheaded Medusa while watching her reflection in a polished shield, so that he never looked at her directly.
In the myth, the winged horse Pegasus sprang from Medusa's body when Perseus killed her.

evidence.restatement: Meeting Medusa's gaze turned a person to stone.
Her gaze petrified people; it did not turn them to salt (that is Lot's wife in Genesis), ice or wood.
Perseus beheaded Medusa while looking only at her reflection in a polished shield.
When Perseus cut off Medusa's head, the winged horse Pegasus (with Chrysaor) sprang from her body.
In the myth, anyone who looked straight at Medusa was turned to stone.
Medusa's gaze petrified; salt is Lot's wife in the Bible, and no Greek myth has Medusa turn people to ice or wood.
Perseus approached Medusa looking only at her reflection in a polished (bronze) shield and beheaded her without meeting her gaze.
Pegasus, with his brother Chrysaor, sprang from Medusa's neck when Perseus cut off her head (Hesiod, Theogony).
